fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The path from festivals to birthkeeping", "body": "Elise Frosch tells Chance Garton how she went from a private Catholic upbringing in Louisiana, hula hooping at festivals and a sociology degree, to a trip to Nepal and yoga teacher training. A friend asked her to be a doula, a word she had never heard, and searching led her to the Matrona program in Georgia. What she expected to be clinical training turned out to be teaching on the physiology and the esoteric nature of birth, and it changed her life in four days."}, {"title": "The case that birth is not an emergency", "body": "Much of the hour is spent challenging the idea that birth is a malfunction needing management. Elise recalls asking her sister, a neonatal ICU nurse, why the cord is cut immediately, and being told the baby must take a screaming first breath or the lungs will not develop. Chance calls that pure superstition, no different from a pitcher adjusting his cap before a game, and says the whole system runs on middlemen who frighten you into needing the expert. Elise adds that hospitals base their protocols on the average American, and she does not consider herself average."}, {"title": "What she says the hospital room does to labor", "body": "Elise walks through the standard sequence: triage, an IV placed just in case, monitors that limit movement, no food because a C section might be coming, and a clock that expects half a centimeter of progress every twenty to thirty minutes. When labor stalls, she says, pitocin brings contractions without the hormones of natural labor, which hurt more, which leads to the epidural. Her argument is that birth is an altered state of consciousness, so bright lights and staff asking if you are okay every ten minutes pull a woman out of herself exactly when she needs to go in."}, {"title": "The unconscious desire to be a victim", "body": "Chance asks whether women have confused the real power of birth with the currency of martyrdom, and Elise says yes emphatically. She points to Yolanda Norris Clark and the Free Birth Society, and to Yolanda answering a question about her painless ninth birth by saying she released the unconscious desire to be a victim. Elise heard that while pregnant with Emanuel and it landed hard. She tells women carrying birth trauma that redemption is possible, but it starts with owning that on some level they agreed to it, a hard pill she knows many will refuse."}, {"title": "Two births and the mystery on the other side", "body": "The stories carry the argument. Elise birthed her first son at home while her mother, once appalled, brought grapes and watermelon and cut the cord. Her second, Manu, arrived in a bathroom with only James there, no midwife, no ultrasounds. Chance closes by reading the C section as astro theology, Caesar and the sun leaving Virgo on December 25th, and by describing the mother crossing into the source realm as father, spirit and child at once, three becoming one."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Elise Frosch of Family Fungi joins InnerVerse to talk about her role as a sacred birth keeper. She helps us conceive answers to the most logical questions pertaining to birth, and we discuss why pregnancy is not a medical emergency, how to dispel fear narratives, the mother as spiritual psychopomp, perspective on the pains of labor, eliminating victim consciousness, and the story of her medically unsupervised home birth experience.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension, Elise details the changes in body and mind during and after the 40 weeks, how not to impart the belief of original sin and brokenness to baby, talking to loved ones about circumcision, hospital SOPs, the mystery of the afterbirth, placentaphagy, and the divine twin spirit guardian.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Birth as an initiation that remakes the mother", "body": "Elise Frosch describes giving birth as a rite of passage written into a woman's DNA, one that arrives without any vision quest and leaves the mother changed for good. She urges expectant mothers to get to know themselves, grant themselves grace and trust their intuition over constant testing, and she reframes so called pregnancy brain as a mind expanding beyond ordinary awareness. Chance Garton links this to the destroyer as regenerator in nature, and Elise adds that pregnancy is a beautiful destruction of false ideas about the self, after which the mother gives birth to life and creates anew."}, {"title": "Original sin read as a misunderstood solar allegory", "body": "Chance Garton argues that the doctrine of original sin literalizes an allegory about the sun's yearly journey into the underworld, where the fall of Adam stands for a seed being planted so that nature can regenerate. He points out that the name Manu, which Elise gave her son, reads as Unam backwards, as in the papal bull Unam Sanctam, and he suggests the exoteric church split the mother's regenerative role off into a devil figure. Elise Frosch connects the idea to how she feels hospitals treat newborns as broken from the first moment."}, {"title": "Talking with loved ones about newborn procedures", "body": "Chance Garton asks how to raise difficult subjects with pregnant friends and family without selling fear the way he believes the mainstream does. Elise Frosch says circumcision is the one issue she has ever messaged strangers about, pointing them to the documentary The Elephant in the Hospital Room, and she shares her objections to routine eye ointment, vitamin K shots and early vaccination. Both describe these as personal views. Chance stresses that in his view every step of a hospital birth is an offer rather than a requirement, while Elise favors leading by example over arguments."}, {"title": "Healthy boundaries for healers, guides and family", "body": "Chance Garton argues that healers and teachers who take on anyone out of fear of scarcity open themselves to being deceived or ignored, and that a firm boundary actually brings better clients through reciprocity. Elise Frosch says these boundaries are why she stepped back from hospital births, and she tells of agreeing to serve as doula for her older sister, whose choices during pregnancy differed sharply from her own. She describes caring for her sister postpartum with love while holding her own convictions, and she believes living the message speaks louder than arguing it with relatives."}, {"title": "The placenta as medicine, inheritance and twin", "body": "Elise Frosch shares how hearing an earlier InnerVerse placenta episode led her to blend part of her second son's placenta into a smoothie and encapsulate the rest, and how an intense anger surfaced that she now views as ancestral healing. Chance Garton frames the placenta as a philosopher's stone formed by a chemical wedding of mother and baby, and offers his own theory that it may be the baby's divine twin or guardian angel. Elise suggests traditional mothers likely ate it fresh, dried it in the sun or charred it, and calls the experience a holy journey."}]
